title: Ezekiel 19:1–14
context: The LORD tells the prophet to take up a lament for the princes of Israel. A lioness raises cubs; one is caught and taken with hooks to Egypt, and another is caught and brought to the king of Babylon. The mother is then pictured as a once-fruitful vine, plucked up in fury, planted in the wilderness, and left without a strong branch to rule. The lioness is variously read as Judah, Jerusalem, or the royal house, and the cubs are commonly identified as Jehoahaz (19:3-4) and either Jehoiachin or Zedekiah (19:5-9). These identifications are not stated in the text, and 2 Kings 23:31-34 and 24:8-15 provide context for them. Both traditions read the chapter as a sober lament over the fall of David’s house.

verses.text: “Moreover, take up a lamentation for the princes of Israel,
verses.arminianNotes: Moreover, take up a lamentation for the princes of Israel, Arminian readers see the LORD directing the prophet to grieve, showing that judgment is not celebrated but mourned.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the lament form is a funeral song. The princes of Israel are commonly read as the last kings of Judah, though the text does not name them.

verses.text: and say, ‘What was your mother? A lioness. She couched among lions, in the middle of the young lions she nourished her cubs.
verses.arminianNotes: and say, ‘What was your mother? A lioness. Arminian readers see a picture of royal strength and dignity, the lioness nourishing her cubs among the young lions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the lioness is variously read as Judah, Jerusalem, or the royal house. Some also observe that Jehoahaz and Zedekiah shared the same mother, Hamutal (2 Kings 23:31; 24:18), though that link is uncertain.

verses.text: She brought up one of her cubs. He became a young lion. He learned to catch the prey. He devoured men.
verses.arminianNotes: She brought up one of her cubs. Arminian readers see a young ruler who learned to catch the prey and devoured men, an image of violent rule.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this cub is commonly identified as Jehoahaz, who reigned three months (2 Kings 23:31-32). The text does not name him, and the identification is an inference.

verses.text: The nations also heard of him. He was taken in their pit; and they brought him with hooks to the land of Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes: The nations also heard of him. Arminian readers see the young lion’s power ended as the nations caught him in their pit and brought him with hooks to Egypt.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers compare 2 Kings 23:33-34, where Pharaoh Necoh takes Jehoahaz to Egypt, and Jeremiah 22:11-12, where Shallum dies in captivity. The parallels support the usual identification without proving it.

verses.text: “ ‘Now when she saw that she had waited, and her hope was lost, then she took another of her cubs, and made him a young lion.
verses.arminianNotes: Now when she saw that she had waited, and her hope was lost, Arminian readers see the mother’s hope disappointed and her turn to another cub, a picture of a nation seeking a new ruler.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the second cub is identified by some as Jehoiachin and by others as Zedekiah. The text gives no name, and both readings have support.

verses.text: He went up and down among the lions. He became a young lion. He learned to catch the prey. He devoured men.
verses.arminianNotes: He went up and down among the lions. Arminian readers see the second cub repeating the first one’s path, learning to catch the prey and devouring men.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the wording deliberately echoes 19:3. The repetition suggests a pattern of successive rulers who followed the same destructive course to the same end.

verses.text: He knew their palaces, and laid waste their cities. The land was desolate with its fullness, because of the noise of his roaring.
verses.arminianNotes: He knew their palaces, and laid waste their cities. Arminian readers see a ruler whose power brought desolation, the land filled with the noise of his roaring.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the details of this verse are difficult, and interpretations vary. The overall picture is of a ruler whose reign brought harm rather than security.

verses.text: Then the nations attacked him on every side from the provinces. They spread their net over him. He was taken in their pit.
verses.arminianNotes: Then the nations attacked him on every side from the provinces. Arminian readers see the nations rising against the young lion and taking him in their net and pit.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the hunting imagery of net and pit. The capture of the second cub parallels that of the first, showing a repeated pattern of judgment.

verses.text: They put him in a cage with hooks, and brought him to the king of Babylon. They brought him into strongholds, so that his voice should no more be heard on the mountains of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: They put him in a cage with hooks, and brought him to the king of Babylon. Arminian readers see the young lion silenced, his voice no more heard on the mountains of Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Kings 24:15 records Jehoiachin carried to Babylon and 2 Kings 25:7 records Zedekiah taken there. The verse fits either reading, and the parallels are not harmonized here.

verses.text: “ ‘Your mother was like a vine in your blood, planted by the waters. It was fruitful and full of branches by reason of many waters.
verses.arminianNotes: Your mother was like a vine in your blood, planted by the waters. Arminian readers see the image shift from lioness to vine, recalling a time of fruitfulness and growth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the vine imagery used of Israel elsewhere, as in Psalm 80:8 and Ezekiel 15:6. The phrase in your blood is difficult, and translations render it in different ways.

verses.text: It had strong branches for the scepters of those who ruled. Their stature was exalted among the thick boughs. They were seen in their height with the multitude of their branches.
verses.arminianNotes: It had strong branches for the scepters of those who ruled. Arminian readers see the vine’s strength as the royal line that produced rulers, exalted among the thick boughs.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the strong branches are read as kings of David’s line. The vine’s height pictures the dignity of the monarchy before its fall.

verses.text: But it was plucked up in fury. It was cast down to the ground, and the east wind dried up its fruit. Its strong branches were broken off and withered. The fire consumed them.
verses.arminianNotes: But it was plucked up in fury. Arminian readers see the vine cast down and dried by the east wind, an image of judgment after unfaithfulness, told without graphic detail.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the east wind and fire are images of judgment. Many read the verse as the fall of Jerusalem and the end of the monarchy, though the poem does not say so directly.

verses.text: Now it is planted in the wilderness, in a dry and thirsty land.
verses.arminianNotes: Now it is planted in the wilderness, in a dry and thirsty land. Arminian readers see the vine transplanted into barren ground, commonly read as exile from the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the image contrasts sharply with 19:10, where the vine was planted by the waters. The change from abundance to drought expresses the depth of loss.

verses.text: Fire has gone out of its branches. It has devoured its fruit, so that there is in it no strong branch to be a scepter to rule.’ This is a lamentation, and shall be for a lamentation.”
verses.arminianNotes: Fire has gone out of its branches. Arminian readers see the ruin coming from within the vine itself, so that no strong branch remains to be a scepter to rule.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that some read the fire from its branches as the royal house’s own rebellion bringing ruin; others read it more generally. The refrain This is a lamentation closes the chapter in grief.
